entities.name: Qin dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Qin dynasty (221–206 BCE) was the first unified Chinese empire, founded by Qin Shi Huang who conquered the six rival states in 221 BCE after centuries of warfare in the Warring States period. Though lasting only 15 years, the Qin's standardization of writing, currency, weights, measures, and road gauge unified China so thoroughly that its political legacy endured for 2,000 years — the very name 'China' derives from 'Qin.'

Qin Shi Huang's standardization reforms were revolutionary: a unified script allowed officials from different regions to communicate; standardized axle widths made roads traversable by all vehicles; standardized bronze weights enabled commerce; standardized coinage replaced dozens of regional currencies. The First Emperor also began construction of the Great Wall to defend against Xiongnu nomads and built a magnificent burial complex guarded by the Terracotta Army — 8,000 individually sculpted warriors discovered in 1974.

The Qin's harsh Legalist governance, book burnings, and massive labor conscription — building the Great Wall, Epang Palace, and the imperial mausoleum with hundreds of thousands of workers — created intense resentment. Revolts erupted within years of the First Emperor's death in 210 BCE, and the dynasty collapsed in 206 BCE after just 15 years. But the Han dynasty that followed maintained Qin's administrative structure, making Qin the essential precedent for Chinese civilization.
